releases.notes:
### Updates

- VPSpilot now updates itself. When a new version is out, an "Update available" button appears in the header with the release notes; one click installs it with a backup, a health check and an automatic rollback if anything goes wrong. `vps-pilot upgrade` does the same from the server.
- Releases are signed, and the server refuses anything that isn't.

### Importing apps

- VPSpilot now scans a repository and detects the apps in it, for Node, Python, Go, Rust, Java, PHP and Ruby projects and for folders with a Dockerfile.
- An import checklist lets you create and deploy several apps from one repository at once.

### Web addresses and security

- Apps get an automatic HTTPS address, either under your wildcard apps domain or on a free sslip.io address.
- The dashboard itself gets an automatic HTTPS address.
- Two-factor sign-in with an authenticator app, with recovery codes.

### Environment variables

- Each variable has icons to reveal and edit its value.
- Typing `${{service.KEY}}` suggests matching services and keys.

### Server commands

- `vps-pilot update admin` changes the admin account.
- `vps-pilot reset-mfa` resets two-factor sign-in.
- `vps-pilot panel-url` prints the dashboard address.

### Builds and deploys

- Apps build with the repo's Dockerfile, or with Railpack when there is none. Nixpacks is no longer used.
- Dockerfiles in a monorepo build from the repository root.
- Builds run one at a time and wait in a queue.
- GitHub webhooks are set up per repository and deploy every service that matches.
- Old builds are cleaned up to free disk space.

### Dashboard

- The dashboard is served compressed and loads in one piece on slow connections.
- Copy buttons also work over plain HTTP.

- Each deployment shows whether it was built from a Dockerfile or with Railpack.
- A domain that routes to a different port than the one the service listens on now shows a warning on its row.
- If two-factor setup was restarted in another tab, entering a code from the old QR code now says so instead of reporting an invalid code.
- Dockerfile apps created from the import checklist no longer get install, build or start commands they don't use.
- Updates are more careful: pressing Ctrl-C during `vps-pilot upgrade` before the swap stops cleanly, and a new update waits until the previous one has fully finished.

### Deployments

- The Deployments tab has a "New deployment" button. Deploy the latest commit of any branch, or pick a specific commit: GitHub repos list the 20 most recent commits, and any repo accepts a pasted commit SHA. The service keeps following its own branch for automatic deploys.
- Deploying a specific commit, including a rollback that needs a rebuild, now fetches exactly that commit. If it can't be checked out, the deployment fails with "Could not check out commit …" instead of quietly building the latest code.

### Importing apps

- `docker-compose.yml` and `compose.yaml` files are imported. Services with `build:` become apps, and `postgres`, `redis` and `minio` images become managed databases and storage with freshly generated credentials. Settings that can't be carried over, and development-only setups, are listed on each row.
- Connection strings that pointed at a compose database are switched to the new managed one.
- Apps can build from a Dockerfile anywhere in the repository, as set by the compose file.
- When a push adds a new app to a project's repository, a banner offers to review and deploy it. Dismissed apps are never suggested again and stay available from "+ New service → From this project's repo".
- A service whose folder disappeared from the repository is tagged "folder no longer in repo". Nothing is deleted.

### Deployments

- Each service has its own build time limit, set in the new Deploys panel. The default is now 30 minutes instead of 20, and it can be raised, set to a custom number of seconds or removed. When a build runs too long, the log says which limit stopped it.
- A new deployment can wait before it replaces the live one, for 10 or 30 minutes or a custom time. While it waits, the old version keeps serving your domains and the new one is on a preview link. "Promote now" switches early. If a newer deployment finishes first, it takes the waiting one's place. Both versions run during the wait, so the service uses twice the memory.
- Rollbacks always switch at once. "Switch immediately" in the New deployment dialog does the same for one deploy.
- Queued and building deployments have a Cancel button.
- Once a repository's GitHub webhook is set up, the panel says "Synced", with a "Re-sync" link in case the hook was changed on GitHub.

### Building on GitHub Actions

- A new build setting, **Where to build**, in the Deploys panel: **This server** (the default) or **GitHub Actions**, for apps that build from a GitHub repository. Building on GitHub saves your server's CPU and memory.
- Setup opens a pull request that adds `.github/workflows/vpspilot-<service>.yml`. Nothing is committed to your deploy branch without you: merge the pull request, then press "Use GitHub Actions". The panel follows each step and warns if the workflow file later disappears.
- Images are built on GitHub and pushed to GitHub's registry (GHCR), then pulled and started on your server the usual way, delayed switch included. A deployment shows "Building on GitHub" with a "View run on GitHub" link, and Cancel stops the run.
- Picking a commit in the New deployment dialog uses that commit's image if it already exists, and otherwise starts the workflow for it. Rollbacks reuse the image they ran before.
- GitHub stops builds after 60 minutes. The build time limit then only covers pulling and starting the image.
- The GitHub connection needs new permissions (workflows, actions, secrets and variables, and reading packages). **Existing users reconnect GitHub once** in Settings. The setup card lists exactly what is missing.
- GitHub's fine-grained tokens can't read GHCR. Add a `ghcr.io` registry with a classic token that has only `read:packages`, or reconnect GitHub: reconnecting grants the package read permission.
- Variables your Dockerfile declares with `ARG` are passed as build arguments. Docker records their values in the image history, so anyone who can pull the image can read them. On GitHub Actions the image goes to GHCR, which is public for public repositories. For secrets, read the `vpspilot_env` BuildKit secret instead: `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=vpspilot_env . /run/secrets/vpspilot_env` (a file of `export KEY='value'` lines).
- Dockerfile builds on your own server do the same for declared `ARG`s. Those images stay on the server.
- Your variables are stored on GitHub as an encrypted Actions secret so the build can use them, and their values are masked in the Actions logs.
- A push builds with the settings saved before it. After changing build settings, the next push or a New deployment uses them.
- Deleting a service removes its settings from GitHub but leaves the workflow file and the GHCR images in place.
- Switching back to This server is immediate. The workflow file stays in your repository but does nothing, and you can delete it. If removing VPSpilot's settings from GitHub fails, the Deploys panel says so and offers Retry.

### Docker image services

- **+ New service → Docker image** runs any image, such as `nginx:1.27`, with private registry logins, volumes, a command, variables, a port and domains.
- Rollbacks run the exact image digest that ran before.
- **Redeploy** pulls the tag again. Tags are not updated automatically.
- Removing a volume from the list never deletes its data. Deleting a service asks whether to delete its volumes, and the box is unchecked by default.

### Registries

- A new Registries section in Settings stores logins for private registries. Tokens are encrypted and never shown again.
